nodes.body: Rell's Gate is the last town before the Deep Road goes under the mountains, and in midwinter it is mostly a lit doorway in a wall of rock. The company is known here, which is new: the gate watch counts you in by name, and somebody has already told them what is wrapped in salt-cloth in the captain's pack. Orr's summons was waiting at the third station and has been read aloud twice since.

choices.label: Report to the Warden of the Deep Road.
Take the company into the Lamp and Ladder first.
Walk the caravan yard and see who is going down.
Go with Nyre to the Reckoning chapter house.
Ask Kettle why she has not unpacked.

nodes.body: Captain Sabinne Orr, Warden of the Deep Road, does not offer anybody a chair. Sixteen Mile Tower has sent no lamp report for five weeks, the couriers are still running past it on schedule, and she wants the tower's road-book brought up the road and put on her desk. She has fourteen Wardens for two hundred miles of tunnel, and she says that number twice.

choices.label: Ask what her patrols found at Sixteen Mile.
Press her for terms worth the walk.
Take the commission as offered.

nodes.body: Her account is short and she does not decorate it. One patrol turned back at the Marchgate without a written reason; the second came home a man short, and the man they lost would not stop counting in a language nobody could place. The Marchgate itself was found unbarred, and the bar was on the inside where somebody had set it down neatly.

choices.label: Press her for better terms now that you know.
Take it as offered; the road will not improve.

nodes.body: Orr has no coin available anywhere in her district and says so before you can ask her for any. What she has instead is the Deep Road oath, sworn on the road-stone in front of the watch, which makes the company Warden-sworn on her road and answerable on it in both directions. It is worth considerably more than money underground, and it cannot be given back afterwards.

choices.label: Swear the oath and take her authority.
Keep your hands free and take the coin instead.
Refuse the road entirely and winter south.

nodes.body: The oath is sworn on the road-stone with the entire gate watch standing out in the cold to witness it, and a clerk enters the Ninth Sword into the Deep Road roll. Dellach's expression throughout belongs to a man who was a Warden sergeant once and never expected to be counted as one again. Nyre records the exact wording twice, in two different books.

choices.label: Go and gather the company.

nodes.body: The commission is sealed at the bottom with wax that will not set properly in the cold. Then Orr gives her condition quietly, as though it were housekeeping: the road-book comes out above everything else, because the lamp hours written in it are the only reason anybody walks that road alive. She has buried four people who walked it on the wrong hour.

choices.label: Ask her for a guide who knows the hours.
Ask to read the tower's last report.
Go and gather your company.

nodes.body: Ossa Vend is nineteen and has walked the Lamp Road twice a week since she was twelve, carrying her father's lighting pole and, since autumn, her father's debts. She wants a half share and the debts cleared, in that order, and she can recite the eleven lamp stations forwards and backwards. She does not ask what happened at Sixteen Mile, which is interesting.

choices.label: Take her on and clear the debts.
Refuse; Vurma can read a dwarf road well enough.

nodes.body: Ossa is hired and her mother's debts are cleared in front of a Reckoning clerk, which takes longer than the hiring. She carries her own lamp-pole and will not let anybody else carry it, and she is on the paving inspecting the first bracket before the rest of the company has finished loading. Vurma approves of her immediately and says nothing.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: The tower's last report is five weeks old and reads as routine until the final page, where the hand deteriorates badly. Folded inside it are the route charts: eleven lamp stations, the hour each is lit and trimmed, and the standing intervals between them. Against the ninth station the tower captain has pencilled four words: the hours have changed.

choices.label: Take the charts and gather the company.

nodes.body: The Lamp and Ladder is half dwarf and half Warden and entirely underground, warm from a flue that runs somewhere useful. A road-mason is drinking steadily through what he saw at the ninth station, telling it to anybody who sits down. The Sable Guild has the table by the flue and is watching the company arrive with the specific attention of people who have opinions about surface companies.

choices.label: Buy the room a round and listen.
Corner the road-mason about the ninth station.
Step in before the Sable Guild starts on Dellach.
Take the company to the bunkroom; sleep first.

nodes.body: A round bought for the room produces the road's own version of the news. The couriers are running the lower march in daylight now, which has never happened. Two Reckoning priests went down in autumn and neither came up, and a coach with southern horses came through in the same week with its curtains drawn and its clerk paying the toll in silver.

choices.label: Follow up the ninth station story.
That is enough for one night.

nodes.body: Sober enough to be exact, the road-mason is exact about the ninth station. The lamps there are lit an hour before the charts allow, and the count that goes with the lighting runs backwards, which no lamp-lighter on the road has ever done. He walked out over the shoulder in snow rather than pass it, and he has not been paid since.

choices.label: Pay him for the whole account.
Write it off as drink and altitude.
Have him take you up to the shoulder tonight to see it.

nodes.body: The rest of it costs him nothing to say and he says it flatly. His mate went on down the Lamp Road to argue about the hours, because the hours are a mason's business as much as anybody's. His kit came back up eight days later on a courier's barrow, with the tools still wrapped in their canvas and the canvas still tied.

choices.label: Let him be and gather the company.

nodes.body: A Sable Guild delver has an opinion about surface companies walking dwarf roads, and he is delivering it in two languages so that nobody in the room misses any of it. Dellach sets his cup down flat, which is how it always begins with him. The Guild foreman watches without intervening, apparently interested in the outcome for professional reasons.

choices.label: Let Dellach answer it with his hands.
Buy the table a round and end it.
Draw steel in a Warden gatehouse.

nodes.body: It takes two exchanges and a broken bench. The delver sits down harder than he intended and stays sitting, and the Guild foreman calls it fair in front of the whole room, which is worth more than the fight. Nyre binds Dellach's hand afterwards and mentions, without emphasis, that he is forty-four years old.

choices.label: Get the company to the bunkroom.

nodes.body: A round is bought for the Guild table and the delver's grievance is heard out in full, which takes some time and involves three separate historical examples. At the end of it he gives you directions to the old drift entrance. He also gives you the name of the survey crew that walled it, thrown in as a courtesy nobody asked for.

choices.label: Take the bunkroom and the quiet night.

nodes.body: A night in a dwarf bunkroom cut into the gatehouse rock, warm from the flue, with the door barred and no watch to keep. The company sleeps properly for the first time since Gallowmere, and it shows in the morning in the way everybody picks up their kit. Ossa sleeps sitting upright against her lamp-pole and denies it afterwards.

choices.label: Gather the company at the bell.

nodes.body: The caravan yard lies under a foot of snow, with one Sable Guild train loading for the lower march and a Rooks banner pitched over the only covered bay in it. A dwarf sits on her own kit at the yard's edge with no company at all. She is watching the Guild train load, and correcting their lashings under her breath, and not offering to help.

choices.label: Talk to the dwarf sitting alone.
Hire the two road-porters looking for a half share.
Cross to the Rooks banner.
Hire nobody; five is enough to feed.

nodes.body: Vurma Kell, pathfinder, was put out of the Sable Guild for filing a report about the ninth station that her own foreman burned in front of her. She made a copy before she filed it, which is either professional caution or spite, and she is candid that she does not know which. She wants a share and a witness.

choices.label: Take her on at a full share.
Offer her a half share and the copy.

nodes.body: A full share agreed, and the burned report's copy handed over unasked before the coin is even counted out. Inside ten minutes she and Ilsabet are arguing about dwarf orthography over the same page, and both of them are visibly enjoying it. Kettle carries the dwarf's kit across the yard without being asked, which is a formal endorsement.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: A half share, taken flatly, with the copy of the report staying in her own coat where she can reach it. She will do exactly what she is paid to do and not one yard further, and she says so in advance so that nobody can claim afterwards to have been surprised by it.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: The road-porters are Halt and Weem, cheap and willing and entirely unbothered by the details of the commission. They have carried for Guild trains as far as the fourth station and never once past it. They mention the fourth station three times during the negotiation without appearing to notice that they are doing it.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: Vasse Corrow has a Warden charter of her own now, bought with what she learned about Kar Duhn from a company that told her nothing and a frontier that told her everything. She offers to take the Sixteen Mile contract off your hands as a professional courtesy. Her tone suggests she expects refusal and would like the refusal noted.

choices.label: Refuse, and drink long enough to learn what she knows.
Sell her the contract and winter in comfort.

nodes.body: Corrow's own autumn, told over two cups and without much decoration. Eleven people went down the Lamp Road under her charter and nine came back up it. Her scout came out of the old drift counting in dwarf, which she does not speak, and died of it eleven days later in a Reckoning bed with the count still going.

choices.label: Leave her the bay and gather your company.

nodes.body: The Reckoning chapter house is cut into the gatehouse rock and kept warmer than the Warden tower, and Prior Enna Vask presides over it with the manner of somebody who has never once been late. On the duty board, in the current hand, is a name Nyre has not spoken aloud since Gallowmere. Ferrin Ostwyn, her brother, posted down the road in autumn.

choices.label: Have Nyre read the chapter's road account.
Draw kit and credit against the commission.
Hear the offer Vask would rather make.
Leave; this is Reckoning business.

nodes.body: Nyre reads the chapter's road account aloud in the flat voice she keeps for bad news, and it takes eleven minutes. Nine deliveries were requisitioned down the Deep Road in nine months, and every requisition carries her brother's signature. Beside each entry, in the same hand, somebody has copied out the lamp hours for the station it went to.

choices.label: Take the copy and gather the company.

nodes.body: Credit against the commission, spent properly on things that work underground: pitch, oil, dwarf candles, crampons, a second reservoir lamp and a coil of wire rope. Vurma insists on the wire rope, refuses to explain why, and then checks the coil twice more before it is loaded. The debt settles in behind the company like a second contract.

choices.label: Load out and gather the company.

nodes.body: Vask's better offer is made kindly and without any pressure at all. Leave the tower alone, bring the Reckoning her own priest's papers instead of the road-book, and the chapter will carry the company's names and debts for nine years, term for term. She says the word nine twice while explaining the terms, and Nyre hears it both times.

choices.label: Sign what Vask is actually offering.
Refuse, and notice that she said nine.

nodes.body: Kettle is in the gatehouse arch with her pack still roped shut, refusing to unpack it and refusing to explain. She has been under one mountain already this year, and the Deep Road is nine hundred miles of mountain with lamps in it. She has been sitting in that arch since the company arrived, listening to the floor.

choices.label: Press her, gently, until she says the rest.
Let her keep it; she has earned one silence.
Tell Orr the company's scout will not go down.

nodes.body: What she says, when she finally says it, is worse than the refusal. The count the couriers are using on this road is the same count she learned at eleven, in the same cadence, with the same pause before the ninth. She has been hearing it through the gatehouse floor at intervals ever since you walked in.

choices.label: Ask her to give you the cadence.
That is enough for tonight.

nodes.body: She sets the cadence out on the table with three cups and a knife, the way the crews did it underground, so that everybody in the company can recognise it in the dark from any direction. It takes four minutes. Nobody says anything at all when she finishes, and Ossa asks her to do it once more.

choices.label: Sit with that a while, then gather the company.

nodes.body: Orr is informed that the company's scout is unfit for the road, and Orr, who is short of people, offers a substitute from her own watch within the hour. A note goes into a Warden roll about a captain who reports honestly. Kettle is on the paving at the bell regardless and does not look at you for two days.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: The last hour in Rell's Gate goes on kit checked twice and the gate lamps lit for the ninth hour by a lighter who does not hurry over any of it. At the end of the yard the mouth of the Deep Road stands open in the rock. It does not look like a tunnel from here; it looks like something holding its breath politely.

choices.label: Go down at the bell, light kit, good order.
Go down tonight, ahead of the Guild train.
Spend the advance properly before you move.
Give the commission back and winter here.

nodes.body: Out at the bell with the Guild train's dust still hanging in the first mile, the road-lamps burning at their proper hours, and eight miles of good dwarf paving underfoot. For the first hour it is the easiest walking the company has had in a year, and everybody says so, and then everybody stops saying it.

choices.label: Take the first junction.

nodes.body: A night start to steal a march on the Guild train means six miles of unlit paving with two lamps between five people, and it works only in the narrow sense that you arrive at the junction first. The company gets there cold, half-blind and already spent on nothing. The day has not begun, and the charts put the next station four hours further on.

choices.label: Take the first junction.

nodes.body: The advance sits on a Warden table with one morning available in which to spend it properly. Nyre wants a hand-barrow, salt and lamp oil, because the road is long and the stations are cold and empty. Vurma wants a second wire line and a moor-iron pick, because the drift is worse than the Guild admits in writing.

choices.label: Barrow, salt, oil and rope.
Wire line and a moor-iron pick.

nodes.body: A hand-barrow, four stone of salt, two casks of oil and a spare reservoir, which together make the most valuable load on the road and by some distance the slowest. Halt and Weem take the handles in shifts and complain in alternation. Nobody suggests leaving any of it behind, then or later.

choices.label: Take the first junction.

nodes.body: A moor-iron pick and forty feet of wire line, cold in the hand and heavier than it looks, bought off a smith who wrapped it without comment. If the old drift is as bad as the Sable Guild says in its own burned reports, both items will earn their weight twice over.

choices.label: Take the first junction.

nodes.body: The first junction of the Deep Road lies eight miles under the mountain's shoulder, where the dwarves put a bench and a lamp and a survey pillar. The Lamp Road goes on straight and lit. The surface stair goes up over the shoulder into snow, and the old drift goes down and west into unlit dwarf work that nobody has serviced in a century.

choices.label: Stay on the lit Lamp Road.
Go up over the shoulder and rejoin below.
Take the old drift and go under it all.

nodes.body: You ride south from Rell's Gate with the oath unsworn and the tower unreported, and the weather closes behind you within a day. Corrow's chartered company goes down the Lamp Road inside a week on terms Orr would never have offered a stranger. What they find is somebody else's story, and nobody ever tells you how it ended.

Up the shoulder at night behind a drunk mason, to look down at the ninth station from above and settle the question. The lamps below are lit an hour early, exactly as he described, and the count that goes with them is running backwards. It is still running when it reaches the two of you, and it does not have to climb the slope to do it.

Steel drawn in a Warden gatehouse puts the whole company in the gate cells before midnight, which is a fast piece of work by anybody's standard. The commission is struck at dawn and passed to the Rooks. Orr reads the forfeiture through the bars in a level voice and does not raise it once, which somehow makes it worse.

The Sixteen Mile contract is sold to Corrow in a covered bay for eighty crowns and a handshake with a witness. The company winters warm at Rell's Gate on the proceeds and is finished as a company by the thaw, because a road town is small and everybody in it knows who sold what and to whom.

Vask's ink dries on nine years of the company's names before anybody has read the clause about her brother properly. The tower is left alone as agreed and the deliveries continue on schedule through the winter. Nyre walks out of her own chapter house without a word, because she has read the clause and will not explain it to you.

The commission is handed back across a Warden table with an honest reason attached, and Orr accepts it without argument because she has been refused before by better-funded companies. You winter at Rell's Gate. Every ninth night, at the ninth hour, something passes under the gatehouse floor counting, and nobody in the taproom looks up.

The Lamp Road proper is nine feet of dwarf paving under a barrel roof, with a lamp station cut into the wall every mile. Every station you pass has been lit two hours before the charts allow, and the brackets have been wiped down. Ossa checks the third one against her father's timings and then stops checking them aloud.

choices.label: Keep to the crown of the road.
Drop into the drainage gallery alongside it.
Stop at the fourth station where a courier's barrow is standing.

nodes.body: The crown of the road runs dead straight for four miles, which means that it can be seen along its entire length by anything at all standing at either end of it. Dellach mentions this once, quietly, and then walks the remainder with his shield off his back and his eyes forward. Nothing appears at either end, which is not the same thing as nothing being there.

choices.label: Press on to the cistern dip.
Get down into the drainage gallery out of the sightline.

nodes.body: The drainage gallery runs alongside the paving at four feet high and full of spring water, which hides the company completely and costs it every yard. Halt and Weem take the barrow through on their knees in relay. By the far end everybody is wet to the waist and moving considerably worse than they were.

choices.label: Climb out at the cistern dip.

nodes.body: The fourth station has a courier's barrow parked neatly against the wall with its load still roped. On the lamp bracket somebody has hung a Warden's shield with the paint scraped off it. Cut into the post below the bracket is a tally of nine strokes with the ninth struck through, and the dust is still sitting in the grooves.

choices.label: Cut the tally out of the post for Ilsabet.
Leave it; the barrow is not your business.
Camp here at the station where it is dry and warm.

nodes.body: The tally comes out of the post in a single wedge of stone, and Ilsabet lays it down beside the mark she carried out of the Barrow Moor last autumn for comparison. The two match stroke for stroke, including a flaw in the third stroke where the chisel skipped and was not corrected. Whoever keeps this count keeps both of them, and has kept them for a long time.

choices.label: Pocket it and go on to the cistern.

nodes.body: At the cistern dip a spring has come through the roof and filled forty feet of road to chest height, which the charts do not mention. The lamps on both sides of the flood are still burning, two of them below the water line, which should not be possible and evidently is. The water is not cold enough to be honest about its depth.

choices.label: Rope a line and wade it.
Go round by the maintenance crawl and lose an hour.
Have Ilsabet crust the surface hard enough to cross.
Cross dry along the lamp brackets.

nodes.body: Chest-deep in spring water at a temperature that ends all argument, with the rope line taut between two brackets and Ossa holding her lamp-pole overhead with both arms the entire way. Kettle counts everybody through twice. The second count is the one that matters to her, and nobody comments on it.

choices.label: Keep the line taut and cross one at a time.
Let go and swim the last twenty feet.

nodes.body: An hour is lost in the maintenance crawl and everybody comes out dry to the knee, which on this road is a bargain. At the crawl's far grating you get the first clear sight of the Marchgate two miles on, and all nine of its lamps are lit, and it is three hours before they should be.

choices.label: Rejoin the road and make camp.

nodes.body: Salt and glass and Ilsabet's flat working voice, and forty feet of cistern crusting over hard enough to bear a man's weight for slightly under two minutes. The company crosses without stopping, because stopping is specifically what the working cannot survive. On the far side she sits down on the paving and will not be helped up.

choices.label: Give her a minute, then make camp.

nodes.body: The surface stair goes up over the mountain's shoulder in a whiteout, cut for dwarves who did not mind exposure and drifted over since. There are cornices on the left hand and nothing whatsoever on the right, and the wind arrives in shoves rather than gusts. Ossa has been over it twice and does not pretend to like it.

choices.label: Rope up and take it slowly.
Push the pace and get over before dark.
Follow the beaten sledge trail somebody else cut.

nodes.body: The slow way is roped in line, with Vurma reading the snow ahead and Ossa's pole probing every step of the drift. Six hours buys two miles and nobody is lost, which Vurma considers an entirely reasonable exchange rate. The company arrives at the old workings with the light going and its legs gone.

choices.label: Drop off the shoulder at the old workings.

nodes.body: The fast way works admirably until Weem puts a leg through a snow bridge over a drainage shaft and hangs in his own harness for eleven minutes while three people work out how to lift him. The saved hour is spent entirely on the lifting. Afterwards nobody suggests that the hour was ever real.

choices.label: Slow down; the shoulder made its point.
Keep the pace and let the shoulder try again.

nodes.body: Something has beaten a sledge trail flat through the drift, days old and as wide as a door, running down the shoulder toward the road. There are small hard bootprints on both flanks of it. The snow in the trail smells of lamp oil, which at this altitude and this temperature is a considerable amount of lamp oil.

choices.label: Follow it and see what was hauled.
Get off it and back into open snow.
Set an ambush on the trail and wait.

nodes.body: The sledge cache at the trail's end has been organised by somebody methodical: Warden kit sorted by type under a snow tarp, boots in one pile and belts in another. Four sledges stand empty and one is still loaded and roped. There is very little blood anywhere in the snow, and the tidiness of it is worse than the smell would have been.

choices.label: Take the Warden signet and the dispatch tube.
Bury what can be buried and let Nyre say the words.
Back off now; the Skree are still on the shoulder.
Follow the small bootprints back to their camp.

nodes.body: A Warden signet and a dispatch tube come off the top of the pile, and the tube is still sealed, which is the interesting part of the find. The seal on it is not a Warden seal at all but a Reckoning chapter seal. Nyre identifies whose chapter it is without needing to look at it a second time.

choices.label: Get off the trail and go to ground.

nodes.body: An hour of digging graves in frozen ground with a moor-iron pick, and Nyre says the words properly over nine Wardens while the company stands sweating in a wind that takes the sweat immediately. Dellach faces uphill throughout. It costs the last of the light and buys something that cannot be spent anywhere.

choices.label: Move before the light goes.

nodes.body: Two hours lying in snow with the cold coming up through everything, and then nine minutes of violence that goes mostly according to plan. Five Skree lie dead along the trail when it stops. One of them is wearing Warden boots two sizes too large and a bone tally-ring of nine strokes on a thong at the throat.

choices.label: Take the tally-ring and get off the trail.

nodes.body: In a drift-filled adit under the shoulder there is a body standing upright, frozen and perfectly preserved. The hands are bound at the wrist in a knot Ilsabet recognises and does not name. A strip of iron has been laid in the open mouth, deliberately, and the snow above the adit has been undisturbed since autumn.

choices.label: Have Ilsabet read the iron in the mouth.
Take the iron and go.
Cover the face and leave the man his iron.

nodes.body: Ilsabet reads the strip by lamplight with her glove off, and pronounces it dwarf-cut, a pay-tally, one of an original nine. The rank cut into the end of it is the ninth hand, the one that keeps the count for the other eight. The die that struck it was cut within the year, she says, because the edges are still sharp.

choices.label: Make camp while there is light.

nodes.body: The old drift goes down and west under everything, unlit and unmaintained, its mouth walled to half height by a survey crew that evidently changed its mind and took its own wall down again. Vurma reads the survey marks and translates two of them. The third she reads silently and then says that it is not a survey mark at all.

choices.label: Walk the open drift where the survey pillars stand.
Take the covered gallery where the roof holds.
Back out and rejoin the Lamp Road at the cistern.

nodes.body: In the open drift the survey pillars stand every hundred feet, and the third one carries nine notches cut beneath the Guild's mark. Beside it a lamp niche holds a clay lamp with oil in it, and the oil has not been standing long enough to gum. Nobody has serviced this drift officially since before Vurma was apprenticed.

choices.label: Take the oil; a full reservoir is a full reservoir.
Leave the niche exactly as you found it.
Duck into the covered gallery instead.

nodes.body: The lamp is decanted into your own reservoir, and it is better oil than anything bought at Rell's Gate. Vurma says what everybody has worked out already: somebody services this drift on a schedule, and that somebody will notice a light reservoir long before they notice five people. She says it without lowering her voice, which is her way of arguing.

choices.label: Push on to the camp ground.

nodes.body: The covered gallery is dry and echoes badly, its roof slabs holding everywhere except the far end where a fall has closed the way entirely. While the company stands looking at the fall, something in the rubble of it shifts once, unhurriedly, with the sound of a chair being moved in another room. Then it does not do it again.

choices.label: Dig through the fall.
Take the crawl on the left of it.
Back out and take the open drift's lamp niche instead.

nodes.body: An hour of moving stone by hand with Dellach and Halt at the face and dust in every throat, until the fall gives up a gap wide enough for a shoulder. Air comes out of the gap immediately and steadily. It smells of lamp oil and old meat in roughly equal proportion, and it is warmer than the drift.

choices.label: Take the gap while the fall is quiet.
Widen it properly first; do it once, do it right.

nodes.body: Sixty feet of crawl on your elbows with the roof riding your back, and then the space opens into a chamber. Nine lamp niches, all burnt dry, and nine hooks above them. Beneath the hooks a Reckoning courier sits in a good winter coat with a chapter seal still pinned at the collar and both hands folded in his lap.

choices.label: Take the chapter seal off the body.
Back out; nine dead lamps is a message and you have read it.

nodes.body: Prior Vask's own chapter seal comes away bright, and the dead courier's satchel holds nine requisition slips signed in a hand Nyre has known since childhood. The last of them is dated eleven days ago, which means somebody has been down here since, and has been keeping the paperwork current.

choices.label: Take it and get out into moving air.

nodes.body: The last camp is the eleventh station, two miles short of the Marchgate, and from its bench you can see nine lamps burning ahead of you in the dark. They have been burning since before the charts say they should. The company's mood has arrived at the specific quiet of people who have stopped asking whether the charts are wrong.

choices.label: Cold camp, full watch, no lamps.
Lamps, hot food and a short watch; they need it.
Send Kettle forward to look at the Marchgate.
Break camp and be at the gate before the hour.
Call it. The road has beaten better companies.

nodes.body: A cold camp with the lamps out, and at the third hour a courier file goes past on the paving below the station. Nine lamps, unhurried, moving in step. At the head of it somebody is counting aloud in a language that appears to have far more numbers in it than any language needs, and the count is the one Kettle set out on a table at Rell's Gate.

choices.label: Let it pass and log the hour.
Follow it at distance.
Leave the porters on watch and get an hour's sleep.

nodes.body: One lamp, hot food, dry socks and ninety minutes of sleep each in a dwarf station with a working flue, which is more comfort than this road usually offers anybody. At the end of it there is something standing at the very edge of the lamplight. It does not approach, and it does not leave, and it does not appear to be breathing.

choices.label: Stand to and challenge it.
Douse the lamp and lie flat until it goes.

nodes.body: The challenge is given in the Warden form, three times, as the oath requires now that you are sworn. On the third asking the shape at the edge of the light answers with a number rather than a name. Then it waits, with what could easily be patience, to see whether anybody in the Ninth Sword knows the next one.

choices.label: Say nothing more; hold and let it go.
Answer it. Give it the next number.

nodes.body: Kettle is back at the second hour with a bad colour in her face and a scout's report in order of importance. The Marchgate stands unbarred with its bar set down neatly inside. All nine of its lamps are trimmed, a scraped Warden shield is nailed to the post as a notice, and the snow inside the arch has boot prints going in and none coming out.

choices.label: Walk up to the gate at the hour and go in.
Wait for the next file and go in behind it.
Send her in alone to open the way for the rest.

nodes.body: The file comes through at the third hour, and the company follows it in at forty paces, moving on the lamp-count off Ossa's charts. Learning the rhythm takes about four minutes and knowing it is worth the whole walk. You arrive at the Marchgate with the leaf still swinging gently from whatever went through it.

choices.label: Go in.

nodes.body: Following nine lamps down a dwarf road at forty paces means staying close enough to hear the count, and close enough to hear one member of the file who is plainly not walking under his own management. After a quarter of an hour Ossa says the thing that everybody has worked out and nobody wanted to be first with. The count is not rising; it is going round.

choices.label: Keep silent and follow to the gate.
Take the count up with them and walk in as one of nine.

nodes.body: The company falls into the file and takes up the count, with Kettle steady on numbers she learned when she was eleven years old. Eleven minutes of walking in that rhythm teaches you the hours, the stations and the intervals better than the charts do. It also teaches you what the file is hauling, and where, and how often.

choices.label: Break off at the gate before the count comes round.

nodes.body: Camp is struck at midnight and the last two miles are walked on unlit paving out of nothing but the captain's impatience. The company arrives at the Marchgate grey-faced, short-tempered and with an hour still to wait before anything can usefully be done. Nobody says anything about it, which is its own kind of comment.

choices.label: Look at what you came for.

nodes.body: The Marchgate of Sixteen Mile spans the whole road: a dwarf arch with a Warden tower cut into the rock above it, its lintel carved with a door held shut by nine irons. A scraped shield is nailed to the post and nine lamps burn on their brackets, trimmed within the hour. The gate leaf stands unbarred and open a hand's width, with the bar set down neatly on the inside.

choices.label: Go in by the open leaf.
Send Kettle up the ventilation shaft and follow.
Have Ilsabet break the mason's postern in the tower.
Sit on the gate and watch it for a full day first.

nodes.body: A day spent watching a gate teaches the company exactly one thing, and it is worth the day. At the ninth hour two men in Warden cloaks that do not fit them come out through the gap, take down three of the lamps, and carry them back inside again. Neither man puts a hand anywhere near the leaf, and neither of them looks once at the road.

choices.label: Enough watching. Go in by the leaf.
Go up the ventilation shaft where nobody counts.
Take the mason's postern.

nodes.body: It is a dry warm camp at the fourth station, out of the draught, with a working bracket and a courier's barrow to sit against. At the third hour the file arrives and stops, and a voice begins a count that includes the sleepers by name in the order they lay down. The captain's name comes ninth on the list, which is the last one it needs.

The lamp brackets are taken as a dry route across the cistern dip, which works for the first three. The fourth comes out of nine-hundred-year-old mortar with two of the company hanging from it. The water underneath is deeper than the lamps had suggested, and it is going somewhere that the dwarves cut deliberately.

The rope is let go in spring water cold enough to stop thought before it stops the hands. The cistern's overflow goes somewhere the dwarves cut on purpose and maintained for nine hundred years. Afterwards the road is exactly as quiet as it was before, and the lamps below the water line go on burning.

The pace is kept and the shoulder's second attempt succeeds where the first only made a point. A cornice gives way with three of the company standing on it, the barrow goes with them, and the whiteout closes over the whole business within a minute. Sixteen Mile is two miles off and nobody from the Ninth Sword covers them.

The small bootprints are followed home to a Skree warren of two hundred under the shoulder, which is about a hundred and ninety more than the plan allowed for. The company is taken alive, because alive is specifically what the warren is paid to deliver. Five more marks go into a tally kept for somebody a long way down the road.

The fall is widened properly, because Vurma is right that it should be done once and done correctly with the pick rather than badly with hands. The gallery roof has been holding for a century with considerable patience. It chooses this hour to stop, and forty feet of dwarf work comes down in the time it takes to look up.

The next number is given aloud, and the shape at the edge of the lamplight accepts it as an answer and steps into the light to complete the transaction. Whatever the Ninth Sword becomes after that is counted, and kept, and moved down the road on schedule. It is not, in any useful sense, a company any more.

Kettle goes in alone at the second hour, and the gate leaf closes to a thumb's width behind her inside a minute. After four hours of nothing at all the company walks back up the Lamp Road without the only person who could recognise the cadence in the dark. That ends the commission, and something else besides.

An hour's sleep, and porters' arithmetic done quietly in the dark. The watch is abandoned somewhere around the second hour, and the barrow goes back up the road with the salt, the spare oil and both reservoirs. The company wakes two miles from the Marchgate with nothing left to walk in with and nothing to walk back on.

The sensible call is made two miles short of the gate, the report is written honestly, and the fee is returned in full to a Warden who accepts it without comment. It is the correct decision. You will spend nine years hearing Corrow's chartered company tell it differently in every station house on the road.

The last quarter mile to the Marchgate runs in the open on dwarf paving, with the arch ahead and the Warden's shield on its post catching the lamplight. Nine lamps burn on nine brackets, every one of them trimmed within the hour. In the snow drifted through the arch there are boot prints going in, and there are none at all coming out.

choices.label: Walk up the middle of the road in good order.
Come at it along the drainage gallery instead.
Send the barrow up the paving ahead of you and watch.

nodes.body: The barrow is sent up the paving ahead of the company as an experiment, on a slight downhill with a rope trailing behind it. It rolls to the arch, stops, stands there for nine seconds, and then goes in through a gap it cannot possibly fit through. The salt and the oil go with it, and the rope comes back cut clean.

From a foot away the gate leaf is dwarf bronze laid over iron, standing open exactly a hand's width. Warm air comes out of the tunnel behind it, smelling of lamp oil and wet stone and something underneath both. The edge of the gap has been worn smooth at shoulder height by traffic, which is not a thing a door does to itself.

choices.label: Go through the gap one at a time.
Lever the leaf wider with the pick.
Take the Warden's shield off the post first.
Knock, and see who keeps the gate.

nodes.body: You go through sideways, one at a time, with the packs passed after and Ossa's lamp-pole passed last. While Halt is still in the gap the leaf moves a finger's width inward, unhurriedly, on no draught whatsoever. Then it stops again, as though it had merely been considering the arrangement and decided to allow it.

choices.label: Get everyone through and form up inside.
Hold the leaf with the pick while the last man squeezes.

nodes.body: The pick goes into the gap with Dellach's entire weight behind it, and the leaf comes open two feet with a groan that travels down the road and keeps travelling for longer than seems reasonable. There is a pause of about four seconds afterwards. Then something a long way below begins, quite clearly, to count.

choices.label: Go in fast, before it finishes counting.
Take the Warden's shield off the post before you go in.

nodes.body: The shield comes off the post in two blows and turns over heavily in your hands. On the inside face somebody with plenty of time and no light has scratched three lines with the tongue of a buckle. Eight hold, nine counts, do not answer to your own name, and the lettering gets considerably worse toward the end of it.

choices.label: Take the shield and go in by the gap.

nodes.body: The tower's ventilation shaft is forty feet of dwarf cut with iron staples up one side, and roughly half the staples are missing at the top where the rock has sweated for nine centuries. Warm air comes up it steadily. Vurma looks at the remaining staples for some time and then says that the rope is not optional.

choices.label: Rope down in order, quietly.
Send Kettle down first and follow her signal.
Climb it on the staples; it is only forty feet.

nodes.body: Forty feet of rope in the dark gets everybody down with skinned palms and nothing worse. The barrow stays roped at the top with Ossa's pole laid beside it, which she does not enjoy. Cold water is waiting at the bottom of the shaft, and it is deeper than the lamplight had suggested from above.

choices.label: Wade out of the cistern room.

nodes.body: Kettle goes down first on a single line with two whistles agreed for clear, which is the arrangement she always insists on and has never once broken. The whistles do not come. There is nothing whatever for six minutes, which is four minutes past the arrangement, and then one whistle, very quietly, from further away than it should be.

choices.label: Go down when her signal finally comes.
Go down now, fast, and find her.
Wait the full ten minutes as agreed.

nodes.body: The cistern room at the shaft's foot is a tank of cut stone holding waist-deep water, with an iron grate at the far end letting into the guardroom. Material has collected against the grate over the course of a season. Most of it is cloth, and most of the cloth is Warden issue, and some of it is not cloth.

choices.label: Force the grate and go through to the guardroom.
Follow the cistern wall to the dry stores.
Take what is caught in the grate.
Dive the overflow and see where it goes.

nodes.body: What the grate has kept: a Warden tally-iron on a thong, a dispatch tube with the writing entirely gone, and a boot with the foot still laced into it. Nyre takes charge of the boot before anybody can say anything about it, which is probably why nobody does. She writes the tally-iron's number in her book.

choices.label: Force the grate and go on to the guardroom.

nodes.body: The dry stores are unlit and smell like a larder, which is the current use rather than the intended one. Nine bodies are stacked with genuine care along one wall, and four pale couriers sleep among them, long-limbed and ribbed like greyhounds. Their hands are folded neatly in front of them in the manner of men at prayer.

choices.label: Withdraw along the wall to the guardroom.
Burn the stores with the lamp oil.
Go through quietly and leave them fed.
Wake them and fight in the dark, on your terms.

nodes.body: Oil, flint, and a store room that goes up like a hayrick. Three couriers die in the fire without properly waking and the fourth goes away down the tunnel screaming in a register that hurts the teeth. The smoke follows the company for an hour and announces its position to the whole tower for two.

choices.label: Move on before the fourth brings help.

nodes.body: Eleven minutes of moving past sleeping couriers at the pace of a minute hand, with Ilsabet laying a salt line behind each footfall and Ossa carrying her pole horizontally. The fourth one opens its eyes as the last of you passes. It considers the situation without moving at all, and then visibly decides not to bother.

choices.label: Keep going and do not look back.
Take the iron off the nearest one's belt on the way past.

nodes.body: The mason's postern is cut into the tower rock round the shoulder of the arch, a dwarf door about the size of a coffin lid, sealed with lead. Beside it in the living rock is a tally of nine strokes with the ninth struck through. The dust from the ninth stroke has not been washed away by anything, because down here nothing washes.

choices.label: Let Ilsabet unpick the seal properly; it will take an hour.
Break it with the pick and go in loud.
Read the tally beside it first.

nodes.body: Read closely, the tally is nine strokes with a running count beneath it in the hundreds, grouped in nines. The lower groups are older than the lead in the door. Vurma stops translating three lines from the bottom and says that the last group is not a count of deliveries but a count of keepers, and that there have been nine.

choices.label: Have Ilsabet open the seal properly.
Break it; whoever keeps that count already knows.

nodes.body: An hour of quiet work: lead cut away in curls, mason's marks answered one at a time in Ilsabet's chalk, and the door finally swinging inward on cold air. The corridor beyond has dust on the floor that nothing with hands has walked through for a very long time. Something without hands is a separate question.

choices.label: Go in.

nodes.body: The postern breaks in four blows, which the tower repeats back to you for considerably longer than four blows deserve. Then a lamp appears at the far end of the corridor, coming up at a walking pace. Whoever is holding it does not hurry, does not call out, and does not appear to be carrying anything else.

choices.label: Take him alive.
Put him down quietly and move.
Challenge whoever is behind that lamp.

nodes.body: The tower guardroom holds a road-scale on its plinth and nine relay chests along one wall, every one of them open and empty. The floor is a mosaic showing a door held shut by nine hands. Three ways lead on from here: the barracks arch, the road office passage, and a gallery from which the smell of fresh lamp oil is unmistakable.

choices.label: Clear the barracks arch first.
Go to the road office; that is the contract.
Follow the smell of fresh oil.
Read the mosaic on the floor properly.

nodes.body: Under the dust the mosaic resolves into something specific: eight hands laid flat against a door of nine irons, and a ninth hand standing apart in front of it holding a tally-board. A border of dwarf letters runs the whole way round it. The border has been worn shallow in places by nine centuries of Warden boots crossing the same line.

choices.label: Have Ilsabet read the border.
Enough floor-reading; the road office is the contract.

nodes.body: Ilsabet reads the border aloud and stops after four words, because it is the same clause the company read on a floor at Kar Duhn, in the same hand. Eight hands to hold the lid, one to keep the count and bring what is owed. The final clause is a price, payable in nines, in perpetuity, and the perpetuity is specified.

choices.label: Take that to the road office.

nodes.body: The tower barracks holds twenty bunks made up to inspection standard, with kit stowed and boots paired at the foot of each bed. The far third of the room has been walled off floor to ceiling with a barricade of shields and bunk timber. It was built from this side, by people who then stayed on this side of it for as long as they could.

choices.label: Take the barricade apart.
Search the sergeant's chest.
Sleep here in shifts; the company is spent.
Strip the kit and the pay chest and go back up the road rich.

nodes.body: Opened just enough to see through, the barricade gives up its contents. Nine Wardens sit shoulder to shoulder along the wall behind it, drained to paper, hands folded, boots off and paired neatly beside each of them. The third from the left is slowly turning its head toward the gap you have just made.

choices.label: Put it down properly and quickly.
Ask it a question.
Wall it back up and walk away.
Cut it free and carry it up the road for Orr to see.

nodes.body: One clean stroke from Dellach, and afterwards Nyre sets the man's boots straight and writes his name in her book from the tag at his collar. She says the words at half volume because there is not time for the whole rite, and she notes that fact down too, in the margin, for her own account later.

choices.label: Go through the sergeant's chest.

nodes.body: The question is asked, and it is answered in numbers, patiently, in the manner of a clerk responding to a query about an account. Eight, it says, and then a pause of exactly the right length, and then eight again. When Nyre asks who the ninth is, the head turns further round and looks directly at the company.

choices.label: Stop there. Put it down and close the wall.
Ask it the ninth question.

nodes.body: The sergeant's chest is unlocked, because there was eventually nothing in the whole tower worth locking away. Inside there is a duty roster with nine names struck out in the same ink, and an unmarked relay key-iron blank. There is also a flask of dwarf spirit with two fingers gone out of the neck and the cork put back carefully.

choices.label: Take the roster.
Take the blank iron.
Share the spirit out; they have earned two fingers each.

nodes.body: The roster reads badly on the walk to the office: nine names struck out on nine consecutive days, the last of them the tower captain's own. Against each struck name somebody has written a single word in the margin, in a clerk's hand. Vurma says the word is the dwarf term used in accounts for tendered.

choices.label: Take the road office passage.

nodes.body: An unmarked relay iron, the same length and gauge as the ones the mosaic shows, entirely blank where the tally should be cut. Ilsabet takes it off you, wraps it in salt-cloth and stows it in her own pack. She does not explain why she is doing this, and she does not explain why she is smiling either.

choices.label: Take the road office passage.

nodes.body: Two fingers of dwarf spirit each, which is not much and turns out to be exactly enough. The company stands in a dead garrison's barracks drinking a dead sergeant's flask, and everybody's hands come back inside ten minutes. Ossa, who is nineteen, is given hers without comment and drinks it without flinching.

choices.label: Take the road office passage.

nodes.body: Four hours of shifts on made beds in a barracks that smells strongly of other men's boots. Nobody sleeps well and everybody sleeps, which is the arrangement, and at the end of it the company is capable of having the day it is about to have. That was not true four hours earlier and everybody knows it.

choices.label: Take the road office passage.

nodes.body: The road office holds a desk the length of the room with nine tally boards ranged along the wall above it. The road-book lies open at its last page beneath a lamp that has been burning for five weeks without being trimmed. In the lock of the ninth relay chest a key-iron stands where a hand let go of it and did not come back.

choices.label: Read the last page before you touch anything.
Take the road-book; Orr wants the road-book.
Take the relay iron out of the lock.
Search the clerk's cubby behind the desk.
Load the relay chests' plate and go back up the road with salvage.

nodes.body: The last page holds five weeks of lamp hours entered in a hand that deteriorates line by line, with nine names tendered against them in a column down the margin. At the foot, in a different pen and pressed hard enough to tear the paper, somebody has written four words. The hours are his now.

choices.label: Take the iron out of the lock and get out.
Leave it all where it lies and search the cubby.

nodes.body: The road-book comes off the desk into Nyre's satchel: four pounds of Warden record and the entire second half of your commission. As it lifts clear, the lamp above it gutters and goes out after five weeks of burning untrimmed. It has the look of a room that was keeping a light on until somebody arrived who could read.

choices.label: Take the iron from the lock as well.
Leave the iron; the road-book is what was asked for.

nodes.body: The relay key-iron draws out of the lock as cold as well-water and considerably heavier than its size argues for. The moment it clears the wards every lamp in the tower dips together, all of them, and stays dipped for a count of three. Far below, something that had been counting steadily starts again from one.

choices.label: Wrap it in Ilsabet's salt-cloth before you carry it.
Put it straight back in the lock and take only paper.
Pocket it and search the clerk's cubby.
Carry it in your mouth, the way the frozen man carried his.

nodes.body: Salt-cloth, then oilcloth, then the middle of the pack alongside Kar Duhn's iron, which Ilsabet arranges so that the two do not touch. The pressure behind everybody's eyes stops at once. That confirms what she suspected at the first door: it was never the iron doing it, it was being noticed through the iron.

choices.label: Make for the stair by way of the schedule board.

nodes.body: The relay iron goes back into its lock, to the quarter turn, exactly as it was found. The lamps steady, the count somewhere below stops in the middle of a number, and the tower resumes its five weeks of silence. The company stands in a Warden office that has just declined, quite politely, to keep any of them.

choices.label: Search the clerk's cubby and get out.

nodes.body: Behind the desk is the clerk's cubby: a cot that has been slept in for months, a jar of clean water, and a private tally scratched into the plaster in groups of nine. At floor level somebody has broken a hole clean through the wall, from this side, and warm air is coming up out of it steadily.

choices.label: Read the clerk's private tally.
Put a lamp down the hole and look.
Leave it; read the schedule board and take the stair.
Go down the hole now, while it is quiet.

nodes.body: The plaster tally is not a record of days but of deliveries, kept in nines for five weeks by a steady hand, with the hour of each written beside it in smaller figures. In the last group there are eight strokes. Where the ninth should be, he has written a single word in common speech, and the word is mine.

choices.label: Go on to the schedule board.

nodes.body: A lamp lowered on a bootlace shows eleven feet of broken wall and then a floor. On the floor is a set of small neat bootprints in the dust, and they go round in a circle. They have gone round that same circle several hundred times without once leaving it, and the dust in the middle is undisturbed.

choices.label: Pull the lamp up and go by the schedule board.
Reach down and take up what is lying by the bootprints.

nodes.body: The lamp gallery holds nine niches with all nine lamps trimmed and full, and an oil store stacked to the roof behind them. A schedule board hangs on the wall in chalk, kept current. Asleep on the bench beneath it is a Reckoning novice in a habit two sizes too large, with a tally-book rising and falling on his chest.

choices.label: Take him alive and ask him everything.
Wake him politely and talk terms.
Kill him and take the book.
Read the board and leave him sleeping.
Put a light in the oil store on your way past.

nodes.body: Brother Cull is nineteen, sent down in autumn under Ferrin Ostwyn, and he is taken with a hand across his mouth and no resistance at all. He is so thoroughly relieved to have been caught by people who ask questions that he begins answering before anybody puts one to him. Nyre gets a blanket round him before the rest.

choices.label: Let him talk it all the way out.
Ask only what you need: the safe way down.
Promise to take him out with you when you go.

nodes.body: It comes out in a flat exhausted voice, the whole of it, with the tally-book open on his knees for reference whenever the dates matter. The hours were changed on Ferrin's written order in autumn. The tower garrison was entered as arrears and tendered over nine days, and the second door at Hollowmarch is nine days from being paid in full.

choices.label: Read the schedule board with new eyes.

nodes.body: He gives the route and nothing else, gratefully and fast, as though speed makes it less of a betrayal. The relay stair is behind the ninth niche. There are two landings where nobody stops for any reason, and there is one hour of the day when the stair belongs to somebody else and must be left entirely alone.

choices.label: Read the schedule board.

nodes.body: The promise is made out loud in front of witnesses, and Nyre writes it in her book with the hour beside it, and the boy's whole posture changes as she does it. He gives up the hours, the stations, the cadence and a warning about the ninth hour, delivered in the manner of a man confessing to a murder.

choices.label: Read the schedule board together.

nodes.body: Woken civilly and offered the chair he is already sitting in, the novice turns out to be a negotiator rather than a victim of anybody. He will give up the stair and the hours in exchange for one thing only. The company carries a sealed parcel up the road, unopened, and leaves it at the Reckoning chapter house without saying who sent it.

choices.label: Accept his terms and take the stair.
Break faith; bind him and ask properly.
Take his other offer: one hour in the file, and safe passage.

nodes.body: The tally-book comes off a novice who never woke up. Nyre's face closes like a ledger at year end and stays closed. Below in the rock the count falters on a number, holds for a moment as though checking something, and then deliberately starts again from one, which it has not done all evening.

choices.label: Take the book and move before the count comes up.
Put on his habit and carry his lamp.

nodes.body: A Reckoning habit that does not fit anybody in the company, and a keeper's lamp held at a keeper's height with the arm straight. It is an adequate disguise against anything that counts by lamp-height and no disguise whatever against anything that counts by weight. Nobody says the second half of that out loud.

choices.label: Read the schedule board.

nodes.body: The schedule board is chalk on slate and entirely legible: nine niches, nine hours, lamps trimmed on the hour without exception. The ninth hour has been ringed twice, and beside the ring somebody has written four words in a very careful hand, which are do not be on the stair. Behind the ninth niche the relay stair goes down.

choices.label: Go down now, well clear of the ninth hour.
Wait for the ninth hour and go down behind the file.
Douse all nine lamps before you go down.

nodes.body: Four hours of waiting in the oil store, and then the ninth hour arrives exactly on schedule. Nine lamps are lifted off nine brackets by hands that nobody in the company looks at directly. A count starts down the stair, and the Ninth Sword steps into the forty paces of silence that follows it.

choices.label: Take the stair.

nodes.body: Nine lamps are pinched out one after another, and the quality of the silence changes with each one of them. After the ninth, the tower is not quiet at all. It is attentive, in the way a room becomes attentive when everybody in it has stopped pretending to read and is waiting to see what you do next.

choices.label: Take the stair immediately, in the dark.
Wait to see what comes up to relight them.

nodes.body: The relay stair lies behind the ninth niche, nine feet wide and cut by dwarves who expected regular traffic on it, dropping away in long flights into the sunless march itself. The air coming up is warm and moving. There is water somewhere beneath it, and above the water a smell like a forge that was left to go out very slowly.

choices.label: Go down in order with lamps lit.
Go down dark, one hand on the wall.
Rope the stair and send Kettle a flight ahead.
Turn around. Take what you have and get out.

nodes.body: Three knocks on dwarf bronze, and the leaf opens the rest of the way from the inside without anything visible touching it. A voice out of the dark invites the Ninth Sword in by the correct number, which is five, and pronounces all five names. None of the five is ever afterwards able to explain why they walked in.

The pick holds the leaf for eleven seconds and then folds along its length, which is what happens to picks used as levers on bronze. The leaf closes back to its hand's width with a man still standing in the gap. The company ends up on both sides of a foot of metal with nothing left that will lever it open again.

The shaft is climbed on staples, roughly half of which are missing at the top where the rock has been sweating steadily for nine centuries. The fourth staple down from the top comes out of that rock with a man's entire weight hanging from it. Below the fourth staple there are thirty-six feet of dwarf shaft and then a stone cistern floor.

The full ten minutes are kept exactly as agreed, because that is the arrangement and she made it. Then the rope comes up with its end cut clean and no scout on it. The company stands at a shaft head in the dark with no way down that anybody trusts and eleven miles of road to walk back up.

The cistern overflow is dived on one breath: eleven feet of cut stone, then a turn the wrong way, then the discovery that dwarves built their drains to be cleaned from the far end and never once from this one. The turn is a little too tight to reverse in, and the light is on the wrong side of it.

Four pale couriers are woken deliberately in a dark store room by a company that had a plan and had rehearsed it twice on the way down the shaft. It survives contact for about eleven seconds. That is how long it takes the second one to come off the ceiling behind the line rather than in front of it.

A relay iron is lifted off a sleeping courier's belt, which takes two seconds and is worth doing. The fourth one decides, on reflection, that it is worth bothering after all. The salt line laid behind the company's feet turns out to have been laid for people who keep walking forward and not for people who stop.

A challenge is shouted down a dwarf corridor and answered correctly in the Warden form, word for word, in the voice of the man whose shield is nailed to the gate post outside. The lamp keeps coming up the corridor at precisely the same walking pace throughout. Nobody in the company manages to move until it is close enough to see by.

Twenty sets of Warden kit and a tower pay chest go back up the Lamp Road on the barrow and sell at Rell's Gate inside a week for genuinely good money. The road-book is still on its desk under a lamp nobody will trim. The receipt in Orr's file records precisely what kind of company the Ninth Sword turned out to be.

A drained Warden is cut out of the barricade and carried up the road on a shield, on the sound principle that physical evidence wins arguments with Wardens. The thing on the shield waits until the second station before demonstrating what it was kept so carefully alive in order to do. It does it to the man holding the front of the shield.

The ninth question is asked, and it is answered. The answer is the company's own names given back in the order they came through the gate, with the hour of each arrival appended. Along the wall all nine Wardens fold their hands in the same manner at the same moment, and then all nine of them look up.

The relay plate is loaded on the barrow and walked back up to Rell's Gate, declared honestly as salvage and taxed at the proper rate by a clerk who counts it twice. Orr reads the declaration without any expression at all. Then she asks the only question that matters to her, which is where her road-book has got to.

The relay iron is carried in the mouth the way the frozen man in the adit was carrying his, because both hands were needed on the rope and the pack was already full. There is no time afterwards to spit it out and explain that the arrangement was purely practical. The iron does not accept the distinction.

ending.title: As the Frozen Man Carried His

nodes.body: Eleven feet down a broken wall into a room where the bootprints go round and round in a circle without leaving it. The circle turns out, with a lamp held low, to have a middle. The middle is occupied, and has been occupied for five weeks, and has been waiting for precisely this arrangement to present itself.

An arm goes through the hole in the wall to take up what is lying there, which is a lamp, and the lamp is still warm. A hand closes on the wrist out of the dark with the unhurried grip of something that has done this before and knows exactly how long it takes for the shouting to stop.

ending.title: What Was Lying by the Bootprints

nodes.body: A light is put into an oil store holding a year's supply, and the gallery immediately becomes a flue. The fire goes down the relay stair ahead of the company, because that is where the air was going. Somewhere below the second landing it finds something that does not object to fire in the slightest and comes up to see.

One hour in the file is agreed for safe passage, lamps are issued, and the count is taken up at the correct number. The hour ends precisely on schedule, exactly as the novice promised. The company is not released, because the file's arithmetic contains no provision whatsoever for anybody leaving it, and never has.

Nine lamps out, and the company waits in the dark to see who tends them. The answer comes up the relay stair without a light of its own, relights all nine from the bottom bracket upward in the correct order, and trims every wick. It takes the trimming extremely seriously, and it takes its time about the ninth.

ending.title: What Comes Up to Relight Them

nodes.body: The stair is declined out loud, in front of witnesses, and the tower is walked back out through the gate leaf into road air. The road-book is delivered and the relay iron declared and taxed. The written report states plainly that the Ninth Sword did not go down the march, and Orr files it, and reads it twice.

Four hundred steps down with lamps lit, and two landings on the way. The wall carvings start as proper mason's work and degrade below the first landing into gouges cut in a hurry by hands that were not holding dwarf tools. On the second landing there is a stair-shrine with nine niches cut into it at eye height.

choices.label: Stop at the shrine and read it.
Straight down past both landings.
Take twenty minutes on the first landing; they need it.

nodes.body: Four hundred steps in complete darkness with a hand on the wall, feeling the carvings change under the palm from tool-work into something scratched. At the ninetieth step something comes up past the company on the outer edge of the stair, entirely unhurried and breathing on a count of nine. It does not touch anybody as it goes by.

choices.label: Press flat to the wall and let it pass.
Strike a light; blind is worse than seen.
Count the steps aloud to keep the company together.
Take hold of it as it goes by.

nodes.body: The stair is roped and Kettle goes a full flight ahead of everybody, working on tugs: one for clear, two for wait where you are, three for come down after me. She gives one, and then another, and then a third, and then two in quick succession that mean nothing in the agreed code. After that the rope goes slack in your hands with no signal at all.

choices.label: Go down fast on the last signal she gave.
Overtake the slack and take the lead yourself.
Haul the rope in and see what is on the end of it.

nodes.body: The stair-shrine holds nine niches at eye height, eight of them containing dwarf tokens gone black with age and the ninth standing empty. The empty one is warm enough to feel from a foot away. The lip of the shrine below it has been worn into a groove by something set down there and taken back up a great many times.

choices.label: Leave the ninth niche empty and go down.
Set the relay iron in the empty niche.
Take one of the eight tokens.

nodes.body: The relay iron goes into the warm niche, which accepts it the way a lock accepts its own key. The whole march goes quiet for the length of one breath. Then the count starts again somewhere below, slower than before and apparently satisfied, and it is no longer paying any attention at all to the stair.

choices.label: Go down and see what you have bought.

nodes.body: A lamp struck on the stair catches the thing on the outside of the flight for exactly one second: a Warden's cloak, a Warden's boots, and above the collar nothing that a helmet would ever fit onto. It continues upward past the company without turning its head at all. Its count does not falter anywhere in the interval, before or after.

choices.label: Go down before it comes back for a second look.

nodes.body: The slack rope leads down two flights to Kettle, who is flat against the wall with her own hand over her mouth, alive and extremely angry about the necessity. She points down at the stairfoot. A Skree haulage gang is crossing the bottom of the stair in file with crates, and it is going to take some time.

choices.label: Wait for the file to pass and go down.

nodes.body: The foot of the relay stair is a crossing of ways in warm moving air. A flooded haulage gallery goes left with lamplight lying on the water; the deep pay-station stands ahead with its doors ajar; a chapel light burns to the right and a pump wheel turns somewhere below it. There is a breach into an old road-shrine, a cutting-shop with a cold forge, and at the far end of everything, a door.

choices.label: Take the flooded haulage gallery.
Open the pay-station doors.
Follow the chapel light.
Go and find the wheel that is turning.
Look into the breach in the wall.
Try the cutting-shop first.
Straight down the hall to the door at the end.
Hail the garrison; somebody down here must be Warden.

nodes.body: The haulage gallery is chest-deep and as warm as bathwater, with lamplight further down it and a flat-bottomed barge poling toward you. Three Skree are aboard, working the pole in rotation. A crate is lashed amidships, eighteen inches of dwarf oak, and it is not making crate noises.

choices.label: Swim the gallery past them in the dark water.
Take the haulage ledge above the waterline.
Ambush the barge from both sides.
Go under and hole the barge from below.

nodes.body: Sixty yards of warm black water with kit held above the head, and the barge pole going past close enough to touch. Halfway across, something long turns over in the depth beneath the company, unhurried and entirely uninterested. It has the manner of an animal that has been extremely well fed on a schedule for a long time.

choices.label: Get out at the far steps and keep going.
Take a breath and see what is under you.

nodes.body: The haulage ledge above the waterline is eleven inches wide, cut for maintenance rather than for men in mail carrying packs. The barge passes below close enough that you can hear the crate being spoken to. Whoever is speaking to it is using numbers, patiently, in the tone of somebody settling a child.

choices.label: Work along it to the far end.
Drop on the barge as it passes underneath.
Take the shortcut where the ledge is broken.

nodes.body: Eleven seconds of violence in waist-deep water puts three Skree over the gunwale, and then there is nothing left to do but look at the crate. Eighteen inches of dwarf oak with air holes bored through the lid in a ring of nine. Inside it, something has stopped making noise in order to listen to you.

choices.label: Open the crate.
Leave it sealed and take the barge down the gallery.
Free what is in it, whatever it is.
Take the gang's lamps and pass as the haulage file.

nodes.body: The crate holds a Warden of the Sixteen Mile garrison, alive, wrists bound in the Compact's knot and eyes bound in Reckoning linen. He is counting under his breath in the cadence Kettle set out with three cups and a knife on a table at Rell's Gate, and he is four numbers from the end of it.

choices.label: Cut him loose, take him with you, and go.
Ask him what he is counting toward.

nodes.body: The lid comes off and the bound Warden is cut free and carried between two of you, dead weight and still counting steadily. Nyre holds his head as they go and tells him, over and over, that the number is wrong. It is the only argument anybody down here has, and he does not stop, and she does not either.

choices.label: Carry him and go on to the door.

nodes.body: Three Skree lamps held at Skree height, and the company poles a haulage barge down a flooded dwarf gallery in the middle of a file that never once looks up. You learn the hours, the stations and the intervals in a quarter of an hour. You also learn what the crates are for, and how many of them there have been.

choices.label: Tie up at the door steps and get off the water.

nodes.body: The deep pay-station is ankle-deep and echoes badly. A rack on the far wall holds eight relay irons in eight sockets with a ninth socket standing empty, and the shift bell waits on its stand beside them. The road-paymaster lies face down across his own desk, and both of his sleeves are empty from the elbow.

choices.label: Turn the paymaster over.
Take the eight irons off the rack.
Read the tally cut into the wall behind the rack.
Ring the shift bell and see who still answers it.

nodes.body: Turned over, the paymaster has no hands and no other injury anywhere on his body. Inside his coat is a confession written by a man holding the pen in his teeth, which takes some time to read and longer to accept. He signed for four years, he says, because the alternative was explained to him carefully, and then he stopped signing.

choices.label: Take the confession and the irons.
Take the confession and go straight to the door.
Look for what happened to his hands.

nodes.body: Up close the rack is warm to the hand and every one of the eight irons sits in a socket warmer than the iron itself. The ninth socket stands empty and worn bright around the mouth. The whole rack is humming faintly, at the pitch a bowstring hums at in the moment before somebody loses their nerve.

choices.label: Take one iron and leave the seven seated.
Leave them all exactly where they are.
Take all eight; the Warden can have the lot.

nodes.body: One iron lifts out, and the rack's hum climbs a full tone as seven irons take up the load of the eighth's absence. Ilsabet says, quietly and with great precision, that the company now has about eleven minutes of the march's patience remaining. She then says that she is estimating, and that she would prefer nine.

choices.label: Go to the door.

nodes.body: Behind the rack the wall carries a tally cut in groups of nine, going back nine hundred years in nine distinguishable hands and then further in a hand that is not dwarf work at all. In the final group eight strokes have been cut cleanly and evenly. A ninth has been begun and left at half its intended depth.

choices.label: Stop reading and go to the door.
Read it to the end; there is a name at the bottom.

nodes.body: The courier chapel holds nine benches and a wall of tally, and at a clerk's desk in front of them sits Ferrin Ostwyn, Reckoning priest, four months into the ninth hand's office. He stands up when the company comes in. He greets his sister by name before he greets anybody else, and he asks after their mother.

choices.label: Hear the offer he means to make.
Ask what the Compact actually pays, and to whom.
Put him down where he stands.
Back out and go and find the wheel instead.
Put a lamp against his tally-wall and burn it.

nodes.body: Ferrin explains the arithmetic the way his order explains debt, which is to say completely and without apology. The thing behind the door cannot be killed and cannot wake while the count holds. Eight irons hold the lid, the ninth hand keeps the count and delivers what is owed, and the road has been paying that instalment since before the Reckoning existed to record it.

choices.label: Let him make his offer, then.
Leave him talking and go to the door.

nodes.body: The offer is made plainly and without any threat in it. Ferrin is forty-one and will not survive another winter of the office, and it falls vacant on his death whether anybody has volunteered or not. For one of the five, named by the captain today, he will give up the iron, the road-book, the tower's arrears and nine more years of the road's peace.

choices.label: Refuse, and go for the door.
Counter: the company will settle this another way.
Accept, and name one of them.
Accept, and name yourself.

nodes.body: The counter-offer is put to him straight: nine irons seated and no hand at all keeping any count afterwards. Ferrin's face does something complicated and entirely human. His order taught him that no debt simply ends, and he has spent four years proving the lesson, and he is not certain enough to refuse.

choices.label: Go to the door with his blessing, such as it is.

nodes.body: Ferrin does not defend himself and does not need to, because the chapel does it on his behalf. Nine benches worth of accumulated dust stands up in the approximate shapes of the people who once sat on them. Nyre's voice goes up for the first time since Gallowmere, and it is not addressed to the dust.

choices.label: Finish him before the benches close.
Break off and run for the door.
Take him hostage and walk him to the door.
Stand and fight the chapel.

nodes.body: Ferrin Ostwyn dies at his own desk in about the time it takes to say a number aloud, with his sister standing over him. The count stops everywhere in the march at once, which is not the same as stopping gradually. In the silence afterwards you can hear eight irons audibly taking up a load they were never meant to carry alone.

choices.label: Run for the door now, while the silence lasts.
Take his tally-book and his ring off the desk.
Wait and see what the count does without a keeper.

nodes.body: Ferrin's tally-book and the ninth hand's ring come off a dead man's desk together. The book runs to eleven hundred pages in nine hands, and the last four months of it are in handwriting Nyre has known all her life. The ring is warm, and it is sized, unmistakably, for whichever hand lifts it next.

choices.label: Take both and go to the door.

nodes.body: The wheel-house under the pay-station holds a dwarf pump the size of a barn, its wheel turning steadily in a race of black water. Three of its nine paddles have been hacked away. A Skree crew is working on the fourth with axes, without any hurry at all, in the manner of people on a long and well-understood contract.

choices.label: Kill the crew and mend the paddles.
Jam the wheel and flood the lower march yourselves.
Cross the wheel-race to the door gallery.
Ride the wheel down and see what it drains into.

nodes.body: A short brutal fight in a very loud room, and then an hour of carpentry with Dellach and Vurma holding a paddle in place while Ilsabet lashes it. The water in the race drops a hand's width by the end of it. The lower march stays dry a while longer, for whatever that eventually turns out to be worth.

choices.label: Leave it running and go to the door.
Stay and keep it running; somebody has to.

nodes.body: The wheel jams on a pick haft and the race backs up within minutes, sending water the wrong way through nine hundred years of dwarf engineering.
